2017_115_112117mtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of November 21, 2017 at the Services Building — the meeting after the sinking fund passed. The one-mill Building & Site Sinking Fund carried the November 7 election with about 68% of the vote, and the Board's sole recognition item thanks the CAPE steering committee that campaigned for it. It then spends the money: $5,299,830.00 of mechanical, electrical and door work at four elementaries under Bid Pack 21, $508,531.00 for the Troy High boiler replacement, $1,448,346.00 for fifteen replacement buses, and $350,778 to migrate the student information system to PowerSchool.
2017_115_112117mtg.page:
**Meeting**
Regular meeting, November 21, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition — the sinking fund passed**
The single recognition item is the **CAPE (Citizens and Parents for Education) Steering Committee**. "Voters overwhelmingly came out in favor of the Troy School District one-mill Building & Site Sinking Fund in the November 7th Election. **The proposal passed with about 68% of the votes**, which is a testament to the support of our parents and the Troy Community." The Board thanks the volunteers whose work "both behind the scenes and in public forums—was integral to the success," singling out **CAPE chair Tracy Heikka**, who coordinated the effort — with the note that "Mrs. Heikka would say it took a team." Certificates go to the committee, among them Rebecca Anders, Nikey Bergy, Heather Blum and Scott & Renee Courtney.

The result exceeds the polling. Epic MRA's April survey had found 61% outright Yes plus 7% leaning Yes; the actual vote came in at about 68%.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the October 3 workshop, the October 17 special workshop and the October 17 meeting, the copy paper bid, and the September 2017 Treasurer's Report.

The copy paper bid (9847) tabulates seven vendors on 4,200 cases: **Paper Express, Inc. at $21.15 per case / $88,830.00** low, then Veritiv $21.90 / $91,980.00, W.B. Mason $21.87 / $91,854.00, Contract Paper Group $21.93 / $92,106.00, Costco Wholesale $21.99 / $92,358.00, Office Depot $22.94 / $96,366.57 and Quill Corporation $31.90 / $133,980.00 — a spread of more than $45,000 on the same commodity.

**Treasurer's Report — September 2017**
Total check disbursements are $8,837,893.61, the General Fund group $7,497,730.74 and the General Fund (101) itself $7,151,239.70. Adding $2,046,585.93 of wire transfers, $255,817.64 of P-Card purchases and $12,516.86 of ACH debits, less $3,995.45 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $11,148,818.59.

**Business — Bid Pack 21**
Mechanical and electrical upgrades at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse, plus door replacement at those buildings and piping replacement at Barnard, Bemis and Wass. Reviewed by Rob Carson and the bond team of TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow. **$5,299,830.00** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund:

| Category | Contractor | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanical (Costello, Leonard, Martell, Morse) | CSM Mechanical | $2,214,668.00 |
| Temperature controls | MCMI | $905,600.00 |
| Door and window replacement (Alts. A1, A2, A3) | Hewett Company | $685,900.00 |
| Electrical | Metro Electric Co. | $597,860.00 |
| Mechanical (Barnard, Bemis, Wass) | Ecker Mechanical | $414,000.00 |
| Contingency | — | $481,802.00 |

**Business — Troy High boiler, Bid Pack 22**
RFP 9846 issued October 15 covers boiler replacement with new boiler venting and circulation pumps, plus electrical service and building automation controls. **Work commences immediately upon award with completion January 2, 2018** — over the winter break. Award: Johnson & Wood mechanical $399,900.00, MCMI temperature controls $50,376.00, Great Lakes Power electrical $12,025.00 and $46,230.00 contingency, **$508,531.00** total from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

**Business — PowerSchool**
The district's student information system, eSchools, **was recently acquired by PowerSchool**. Beth Soggs' November 14 memo makes the scale argument: PowerSchool's SMS package represents **over 735,000 students across 455 districts** in Michigan — every district in Macomb County plus Birmingham, Lake Orion, Oxford and West Bloomfield in Oakland — against eSchools' **42,000 students across 11 districts**.

The five stated reasons for migrating: staff and parent concerns with eSchools; the ability to collaborate with neighboring districts on reports, training and integrations; online registration and forms; single sign-on for parents reaching Schoology, payments, attendance and report cards; and improved parent and teacher portals. Demonstrations were held for administrative staff and secondary scheduling staff with positive feedback. Award: **$350,778**, spread over 2017-18, 2018-19 and 2019-20, from the General Fund.

**Business — buses**
**Fifteen** of the district's buses have reached end-of-life — up from ten the previous January. Using the MSBO cooperative purchasing service, three proposals were reviewed with Transportation Liaison Dominick Asaro; low bidder **Hoekstra Transportation** is awarded **$1,448,346.00** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund under the School Bus Replacement Program, 2016 Bond Series 2. The specification covers four types: 2 conventional 77-passenger, 5 special-needs 53-passenger with child integrated seating, 4 48-passenger with child integrated seating and 4 rear-engine 78-passenger.

**Other**
Trustee Gary Hauff is approved to attend the NSBA Advocacy Institute in Washington, D.C., February 4-6, 2018.

**Recognition 2.A: the CAPE steering committee.** The item opens: "As you no doubt have heard, voters overwhelmingly came out in favor of the Troy School District one-mill Building & Site Sinking Fund in the November 7th Election. The proposal passed with about 68% of the votes, which is a testament to the support of our parents and the Troy Community. The results exemplified their faith in our schools and the value they see in the exemplary education we provide for the students of this District. We are very grateful for their confidence in the fiscal responsibility of our Board of Education and their trust in our stewardship of their investment."

It goes on: passage of the Sinking Fund could not have come without the tireless work of many people — parents, community volunteers, staff and administrators — and the Board wishes to personally thank the driving force behind it, the Steering Committee of CAPE, Citizens and Parents for Education, who volunteered countless hours to ensure the initiative passed. Their dedication and hard work, both behind the scenes and in public forums, was integral to the success of the proposal. The item especially acknowledges CAPE chair Tracy Heikka, who coordinated the group's efforts and worked tirelessly to ensure the measure passed, adding that "Mrs. Heikka would say it took a team." Names are read and certificates passed out, with Heikka invited up at the end to say a few words if she wishes. The committee members named include Rebecca Anders, Nikey Bergy, Heather Blum and Scott & Renee Courtney.

The outcome is worth setting against the packets that led to it. The Epic MRA survey delivered to the Board on June 13, 2017 tested a 1-mill proposal and found 61% Yes with a further 7% leaning Yes, warning across three separate slides that tax neutrality was what earned the community's endorsement and that raising the ask would collapse support. The Board placed exactly one mill on the ballot on July 18, over Mrs. Hammond's lone dissent, certifying the language by the August 15 deadline. The measure carried at about 68% — at or slightly above the survey's combined yes-and-leaning-yes, and comfortably above its outright yes.

**Consent agenda.** Minutes of the October 3, 2017 workshop; minutes of the October 17, 2017 special workshop; minutes of the October 17, 2017 board meeting; the copy paper bid; and the Treasurer's Report for September 2017.

**Consent item 5.D: copy paper bid.** Todd Hensley's November 7, 2017 memorandum covers BID 9847, copy paper for the 2017-18 school year. The bid tabulation, dated November 6, 2017, prices 4,200 cases from seven vendors: Contract Paper Group at $21.93 per case for $92,106.00; Costco Wholesale at $21.99 for $92,358.00; Office Depot, Inc. at $22.94 for $96,366.57; Paper Express, Inc. at $21.15 for $88,830.00; Quill Corporation at $31.90 for $133,980.00; Veritiv Operating Company at $21.90 for $91,980.00; and W.B. Mason Co., Inc. at $21.87 for $91,854.00.

Six of the seven cluster within about eighteen cents a case; Quill's bid is roughly ten dollars a case above the field, a difference of more than forty-five thousand dollars on the same commodity. Paper Express is low.

**Treasurer's Report, September 2017.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $7,151,239.70, with Total General Fund of $7,497,730.74 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $8,837,893.61. Adding ACH debits of $12,516.86, outgoing wire transfers of $2,046,585.93 and P-Card purchases of $255,817.64, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $3,995.45, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $11,148,818.59. The middle sections of the packet are the September check register run by fund.

**Business 8.A: mechanical and electrical upgrades and door replacements, Bid Pack 21.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on mechanical and electrical upgrades at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse Elementary Schools. The bid also included door replacement work at those buildings along with piping replacement work at Barnard, Bemis and Wass Elementary Schools. Bid responses were reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations, and the bond team of TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow.

The resolution awards bid pack 21 in the amount of $5,299,830.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, allocated as: CSM Mechanical, mechanical work at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse, $2,214,668.00; MCMI, temperature controls, $905,600.00; Hewett Company with alternates A1, A2 and A3, door and window replacement, $685,900.00; Metro Electric Co., electrical, $597,860.00; Ecker Mechanical, mechanical at Barnard, Bemis and Wass, $414,000.00; and a contingency budget of $481,802.00.

This is the largest single award in the 2017 packets and one of the largest in these records. Its scope maps directly onto the district's bond program sequencing: Barnard, Bemis and Wass had received mechanical and electrical upgrades under Bid Pack 18 in December 2016 and are here receiving hydronic piping replacement, while Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse take their turn for the unit ventilators, HVAC and electrical work. The August 2018 bond and sinking fund update would list both as in-process 2018 projects.

**Business 8.B: Troy High School boiler replacement, Bid Pack 22.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on the Troy High boiler replacement, reviewed by Rob Carson and the same bond team. Carson's November 8, 2017 memorandum records that RFP Bid 9846 was issued on October 15, 2017; that the scope of work is to perform boiler replacement with new boiler venting and circulation pumps along with electrical service and building automation controls for the new boilers; and that the work will commence immediately upon award with a completion of January 2, 2018.

The RFP specified 3 bid categories. Carson recommends, on low bid per category: category 230000 mechanical, Johnson & Wood, $399,900.00; category 230900 temperature controls, MCMI, $50,376.00; and category 260000 electrical, Great Lakes Power, $12,025.00; plus a contingency budget of $46,230.00, for a total budget recommendation of $508,531.00. All proposals were reviewed and qualified by the bond team, with a separate purchase order to be issued for each bid category. The resolution awards bid pack 22 in the amount of $508,531.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

The January 2 completion date is the point of the schedule: a high school's boilers can only be replaced in the window when the building is empty and still needs to be warm enough not to freeze, which in Michigan means the six weeks between award and the return from winter break.

**Business 8.C: PowerSchool contract.** The district currently uses eSchools as its student information management system, and eSchools was recently acquired by PowerSchool. PowerSchool has an SMS package widely used across Michigan, and there are many benefits to migrating.

Beth Soggs' November 14, 2017 memorandum to the Board makes the case in terms of market position. PowerSchool's SMS package represents over 735,000 students across 455 districts in Michigan; all districts in Macomb County use PowerSchool, as do four districts in Oakland County — Birmingham, Lake Orion, Oxford and West Bloomfield. In comparison, eSchools currently represents 42,000 students across 11 districts in Michigan.

The district plans to migrate for five stated reasons: staff and parent concerns with eSchools; the ability to collaborate with neighboring districts on reports, training, integrations and the like; online registration and forms; single sign-on for parents to access student information items such as Schoology, payments, attendance and report cards; and improved parent and teacher portals, HAC and TAC. Demonstrations were held for administrative staff and the staff responsible for secondary scheduling, and feedback from attendees was positive.

The resolution awards the student management system to PowerSchool in the amount of $350,778 as an expenditure of the General Fund, with the cost spread over the 2017-18, 2018-19 and 2019-20 school years.

The underlying situation is a vendor consolidation rather than a competitive procurement: the district's incumbent system was bought by a larger competitor, and the practical choice became whether to migrate to the acquirer's flagship product or remain on a platform serving a twentieth as many Michigan students. The collaboration argument — shared reports, training and integrations with neighboring districts — is a real benefit of that concentration, and the same logic that made eSchools acquirable.

**Business 8.D: bus purchase.** Fifteen of the district's school buses have reached end-of-life. The Michigan School Business Officials School Bus Purchasing Program was used to obtain competitive pricing, compared and reviewed by Mr. Dominick Asaro, Transportation Liaison.

Todd Hensley's November 9, 2017 memorandum, headed School Bus Replacement Program – 2016 Bond Series 2 – 2017-18 School Year, records that fifteen of the district's fleet have reached their end-of-life cycle; that MSBO offers a cooperative bus purchasing service to obtain competitive pricing from bidding dealers; that the service was used to obtain pricing for several models matching the district's needs; and that after analyzing three proposals and reviewing them with Asaro, they collaboratively recommend the low bidder, Hoekstra Transportation, at $1,448,346.00. The resolution awards the school bus purchase to Hoekstra Transportation in that amount as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

The bid tabulation specifies four bus types with quantities: 2 conventional 77-passenger; 5 53-passenger special needs with child integrated seating; 4 48-passenger with child integrated seating; and 4 rear-engine 78-passenger. Nine of the fifteen buses — the 53-passenger special needs and 48-passenger units, both with child integrated seating — are configured for students with disabilities.

This is the second bus purchase in these packets from the same vendor in the same calendar year: ten buses awarded in February 2017 under 2014 Bond Series 2, and fifteen here at $1,448,346.00 under 2016 Bond Series 2 — twenty-five buses replaced in ten months.

**Other 10.A: 2018 NSBA Advocacy Institute.** As required by Board Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board; Reimbursement of Expenses, any expenditure of district funds for members for out-of-state meetings must have prior approval by resolution. Board Trustee Gary Hauff has indicated his desire to attend the National School Boards Association Advocacy Institute Conference in Washington, D.C., February 4-6, 2018, and the resolution approves his attendance as a representative of the Troy Board of Education. Hauff would return to the same conference the following year, approved in October 2018 alongside Trustee Elizabeth Hammond for the January 27-29, 2019 institute.

Read as a whole, the November 2017 packet is the district turning a mandate into contracts. Two weeks after voters approved a one-mill sinking fund at about 68%, the Board thanks the volunteer committee that ran the campaign and then, in the same sitting, commits $5,299,830.00 to four elementary schools' mechanical and electrical systems, $508,531.00 to a boiler replacement scheduled around the winter break, $1,448,346.00 to fifteen buses of which nine are configured for students with disabilities, and $350,778 to move its student records onto the platform that had just acquired its vendor. The smallest item on the agenda — 4,200 cases of copy paper — is decided by a $45,000 spread between the cheapest and dearest bidder for an identical product.
